item.title: Inuyama Castle: Japan's Oldest Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Inuyama Castle, completed in 1537 on a bluff above the broad Kiso River, holds what is generally considered Japan’s oldest surviving original castle keep, one of only a dozen that escaped demolition, fire and war — and one of just five designated National Treasures. Climbing its steep, creaking wooden stairs is a walk through unrestored history that ends on a top-floor balcony with sweeping views over the river to the mountains of Gifu, and each spring several hundred cherry trees ring the castle hill and the old town below, making the season’s festival the prettiest time to visit.

item.title: Inuyama Cormorant Fishing: Firelit Nights on the Kiso River — Guide
item.description: Ukai, the ancient art of fishing with trained cormorants, has been practised on the Kiso River for some 1,300 years, and Inuyama’s summer performances unfold in one of its finest settings — the dark river beneath the floodlit silhouette of Japan’s oldest castle keep. From June to mid-October, spectators board wooden yakata boats hung with lanterns and drift alongside the fishing craft as usho masters in traditional grass skirts and ceremonial dress work a dozen leashed birds by the light of blazing pine-fire baskets, the flames, splashing and handlers' calls conjuring a scene unchanged for centuries.

item.title: The Kiso River: Japan's Rhine Below Castle and Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Kiso River flows down from the Kiso Valley of the Central Alps to sweep past Inuyama in a broad, green corridor that a Meiji-era geographer famously nicknamed the ‘Japanese Rhine’ — like the German river, it pairs castle-crowned bluffs with vine-green gorges and long gravel shoals. The Inuyama reach is the scenic heart: National Treasure Inuyama Castle rises directly above the water, sightseeing boats and seasonal cormorant-fishing cruises work the current, and riverside paths make for easy cycling and strolling, while upstream the river threads toward the old Nakasendo post towns of Tsumago and Magome on the Gifu-Nagano border.
